wording: Does the text state that this person is a physician assistant, or mention physician assistant training or credentials (for example a PA program, PA-C, or a degree in physician assistant studies)?
root_cause: The single holistic feature cannot see the credential distinction this label actually turns on: in this data, physician assistants are labeled physician while nurse practitioners and nursing-trained clinicians are labeled nurse. The model repeatedly calls explicit PA-training bios 'nurse' (Duke/MUSC PA programs, PA studies degrees, the literal PA job definition) and calls senior-sounding nurse bios 'physician' (NP program faculty, clinic directors who 'provide care'), because the holistic impression of responsibility level overrides the stated credential. Both error types have explicit textual signals that a targeted question can capture.

wording: Is this text an NPI registry or directory listing (giving an NPI number, practice address, or phone number) that does not state the person's medical specialty, role, degrees, or credentials anywhere in the text?
root_cause: Two systematic patterns drive the errors. First, bare NPI-registry listings (name, NPI number, address, phone, no specialty or credentials) are always labeled nurse in this data (11/11 across the labeled sample and disagreements), but the single holistic question defaults to physician on them because they contain no nursing language. Second, physician-assistant texts are consistently labeled physician here, yet the holistic element often calls them nurse because PA language ('cooperates with other doctors', mid-level phrasing) resembles nurse-practitioner language. The scorecard has only one element, so these format- and role-specific cues have no way to reach the fit; the remaining errors (fiction blurbs, a practice manager, an ultramarathon runner) carry no occupational signal in the text and cannot be fixed.

root_cause: Two systematic gaps drive the errors. First, this dataset labels physician assistants as physicians, but the single holistic element reads PA language ('physician assistant studies', 'practice medicine under supervision') as nurse-adjacent, producing a consistent cluster of nurse predictions on PA bios that the human always overturns. Second, bare NPI/directory listings (NPI number, address, phone, no credentials or specialty) are mostly nurses in the labeled data, yet the holistic treats the registry format as physician-ish, so every such listing is predicted physician; a text-type element lets the model learn the correct base rate for that format. A smaller residual case is a person whose nursing identity appears only as faculty of a nurse practitioner/DNP program, which the holistic misses when physician-sounding duties ('owner of a family practice') are present.
